title: Travel
subtitle: Border crossings and airport security put your devices under a level of scrutiny that doesn't usually apply in most situations. This guide walks through different steps you can take to protect your privacy as much as possible while traveling in and out of the US.

context.title: Fourth Amendment rights at the border
context.body: Border agents in the US can search or seize any electronic device without a warrant or probable cause, regardless of your immigration status. What changes based on your status is what happens if you decline to grant access to your devices. US citizens cannot be denied entry for refusing a device search, though the device can be held and you may face a long delay. Green card holders generally cannot be denied entry either, but may face further questioning or deportation proceedings. Visa holders and other visitors can be denied entry outright for refusing to comply.
context.body2: This is not legal advice. If you have reason to believe you'll be a target due to your work, your public profile, or your immigration status, speak with an immigration or civil rights attorney before you travel.

warning.body: This guide is written for general travel and border-crossing security. If you're undocumented or have an uncertain immigration status, your risk profile is different and this guide might not be right for your situation. We recommend consulting with an immigration attorney or an organization that specializes in immigrant rights before you travel.

items.name: Update your devices
items.why: An out-of-date operating system is one of the biggest gaps in your device's security. Every update closes off exploits that forensic extraction tools rely on to bypass your PIN / password. Buying a secondary device isn't realistic for most people, so making sure your everyday device is fully up to date is an important step before your trip.

steps.text: iPhone: `Settings` → `General` → `Software Update`
Android: `Settings` → `System` → `System update` (path varies slightly by manufacturer; search for `System update` if you can't find it)
MacOS: `System Settings` → `General` → `Software Update`
Windows 11: `Settings` → `Windows Update` → `Check for updates`

items.name: Enable device encryption
items.why: Encryption is the backbone of data security and privacy. Many devices and their backups are not encrypted by default and must be manually configured.

steps.text: iPhone: `Settings` → `Your Name` → `iCloud` → `Advanced Data Protection` → follow the prompts
Advanced Data Protection activates end to end encryption (e2ee) for all of your iCloud backups
MacOS: `System Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → scroll to `FileVault` → toggle it on
Save the recovery key somewhere safe like a password manager or fire safe - do NOT store it directly on your laptop
Windows Home: `Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → `Device encryption` → follow the prompts
Windows Pro: search for `BitLocker` in the Start menu → `Manage BitLocker` → `Turn on BitLocker` choose full drive if prompted
Save the recovery key somewhere safe like a password manager or fire safe - do NOT store it directly on your laptop

sources.label: Digital Privacy at the U.S. Border - Electronic Frontier Foundation

items.name: Set a strong password
items.path: Settings → Passcode / Screen Lock (varies by device)
items.why: A strong password is one of the best defenses against unwanted intrusion into your devices and accounts. Avoid using names, birthdays, social security numbers, or other personal information in your password. At minimum, aim to have passwords that are at least 8-10 characters long, and use a phrase that's difficult to guess. For example, 'WeLooked@TheMoon75.' For extra security, you can use a randomly generated password that you then memorize.

steps.text: iPhone: `Settings` → `Face ID & Passcode` → `Change Passcode` → `Passcode Options` → choose `Custom Numeric Code` or `Custom Alphanumeric Code`
Android: `Settings` → `Security` → `Screen Lock` → choose `PIN` or `Password`
MacOS (not iCloud): `System Settings` → `Touch ID & Password` → `Change...`
Windows: `Settings` → `Accounts` → `Sign-in options` → `Password` → `Change`

items.name: Back up your devices before you leave
items.why: If a device is seized, damaged, or you factory reset it, a recent backup will allow you to recover everything once you're through.

steps.text: iPhone: `Settings` → `Your Name` → `iCloud` → `iCloud Backup` → `Back Up Now`
Samsung Galaxy: `Settings` → `Your Name` → `Samsung Cloud` → `Back up data`
Google Pixel: `Settings` → `System` → `Backup` → `Back up now`
Google Pixel Photos: `Photos` → `Your Profile icon` → `Settings` → `Backup and sync`

MacOS Time Machine: connect an external storage drive to your Mac that has at least twice the storage space → `System Settings` → `General` → `Time Machine` → `Add Backup Disk` → select your storage drive → `Set Up Disk` → follow the prompts
MacOS iCloud: `System Settings` → `Your Name` → `iCloud` → `Manage` → choose the apps to back up
Windows: `Start` → search for backup → `Windows Backup` → choose the `Folders`, `Apps`, `Settings`, and `Credentials` you wish to back up
Optional for laptops: back up to an encrypted external drive or a cloud provider

items.name: Know your rights
items.path: Applies at any US border crossing
items.why: Knowing your rights in advance and practicing them before you need them is the best way to stay cool under pressure. Keep in mind that even for US citizens, refusal to hand over device passwords will likely prompt CBP agents to detain you for an extended period of time.

steps.text: US citizens: cannot be denied entry into the US, must answer identity and citizenship questions, can decline device searches, can decline handing over device passwords
Green card holders: generally cannot be denied entry without an immigration judge hearing, can decline device searches, but may face further questioning or deportation proceedings
Visa holders and other visitors: can be denied entry for declining to answer questions or allow a device search
If questioned, tell the truth and do not misrepresent anything
If your device is seized, ask for a receipt so you have a record to follow up on later

sources.label: Can Border Agents Search Your Electronic Devices? - ACLU

items.name: Remove sensitive apps and data
items.why: Treat any data on your phone as potentially accessible by anyone who has physical access to your phone. Remove anything that contains personal or sensitive information. This mainly protects against someone browsing through your device by hand as it does not fully protect against a forensic tool recovering deleted data.

steps.text: Consider uninstalling email, calendar, document, and messaging apps that hold sensitive content on your phone and laptop
Delete individual sensitive text threads, notes, or photos
Be sure to empty the trash or recently-deleted folder afterward. Deleted items are often recoverable for a period of time
Disable location history in map apps

items.name: Leave and delete all Signal groups
items.path: Signal → Group → Leave group, then delete the thread
items.why: Even if you uninstall Signal (detailed in the next step), it's good practice to leave Signal groups in advance of your travel for an additional layer of privacy.

steps.text: Open the group in Signal → tap the group name → `Leave group`
Then swipe left on the thread from the main screen and delete it to remove its history
Make a note beforehand of which groups you'll need to be re-added to afterward

items.name: Back up and uninstall Signal
items.why: Signal conversations are often exactly the kind of content you'd most want protected. Back up and then delete the app before you travel.

steps.text: Open Signal → your profile → `Settings` → `Backups` → enable backups
Save the recovery key somewhere safe like a password manager or fire safe - do NOT store it directly on your phone
Confirm the recovery key when prompted, then tap `Back Up Now`
Delete the Signal app from your phone (and desktop if installed) once the backup completes
To restore afterward: reinstall Signal, confirm your number, choose `Restore from Backup`, and enter your recovery key

items.name: Sign out of your accounts on phone and laptop
items.path: Email, cloud storage, social media, forums
items.why: Being signed out gives you stronger footing to decline providing a password, since there's no active session sitting open for someone to browse through.

steps.text: Sign out of email and calendar apps on both your phone and laptop
Sign out of cloud storage (Google Drive, iCloud, OneDrive, etc)
Sign out of social media apps and any forums you're signed into

items.name: Set social media accounts to private or deactivate them
items.why: Border agents and visa reviewers can look up your public social media presence without ever touching your device. If you're applying for a visa, this needs to happen well before you apply since there's evidence of prior online activity being reviewed as part of the application itself.

steps.text: Set accounts to private, or deactivate them temporarily, on any platform where you have a public presence
You are not required to provide social media handles to border agents. You can decline to answer and don't have to explain why
If applying for a visa, lock down or clean up your profiles as early as possible in the process, not right before travel

items.name: Protect your password manager
items.path: Travel mode, or back up and remove entirely
items.why: Your password manager is a single point of access to nearly every account you have. Some password managers offer a dedicated travel mode (like 1Password) that temporarily hides vaults rather than requiring you to uninstall anything.

steps.text: If your password manager supports a travel mode, enable it for all vaults except what you need for the trip itself
Otherwise, make sure your master password is memorized and your account recovery key is safely written down before removing the app from your devices
Do NOT remove authenticator app codes used for two-factor authentication. They are difficult to restore and aren't useful without your password anyway

items.name: Power off devices before reaching security checkpoints
items.why: A device is at its most secure before it's unlocked for the first time after booting. Powering it off ensures your phone is in this state when it's time turn it back on. Once a passcode has been entered to unlock your phone, extraction tools have an easier time bypassing encryption.

steps.text: iPhone: hold the power button and volume-down button together, then slide to power off
Highly recommended for iPhone: activate Lockdown Mode first → `Settings` → `Privacy & Security` → `Lockdown Mode`
Android: hold the power button, then select power off
MacOS: `Apple icon` → `Shut down...`
Windows: `Start` → click the power icon → `Shut down`
Do all of these before you reach the security line

items.name: Disable Face ID or fingerprint
items.path: Settings → Face ID & Passcode (iPhone) / Settings → Security (Android)
items.why: Some courts have treated biometric unlock differently from a memorized password, and you may legally be compelled to use biometrics to unlock your device. If you plan to have your phone turned off, this step is not as necessary as all phones require your password when you try to unlock them for the first time after rebooting.

steps.text: iPhone: `Settings` → `Face ID & Passcode` → turn off `Use Face ID for iPhone Unlock`
Biometrics are required to enable Advanced Data Protection, so this is not an option for users who have that turned on
Android: `Settings` → `Security` (or `Lock Screen`) → `Biometrics` → turn off face and fingerprint unlock
iPhone quick-lock: press the power button 5 times rapidly, or hold the side button with a volume button, to force a passcode prompt on next unlock
Android quick-lock: hold the power button then select Lockdown to temporarily disable biometrics

items.name: Print boarding passes and travel documents
items.path: Print at home or at the airport
items.why: Keeping paper copies of your boarding pass and other travel documents means you can go through security and customs with your phone powered off.

steps.text: Print your boarding pass at home, or at a kiosk when you arrive at the airport
For visas, customs forms, or other travel documents, you may need to plan ahead. Some countries only offer these digitally, so verify before your trip

items.name: Opt out of facial recognition
items.path: Say it before handing over your ID
items.why: US citizens have the right to opt out of facial recognition scans at TSA checkpoints. Declining doesn't slow you down meaningfully and avoids adding your face to another biometric database.

steps.text: Say "I want to opt out of facial recognition" before handing over your ID
This applies at security, at some boarding gates, and at passport control
You'll still need to show your ID so the agent can visually compare your face to your photo

sources.label: Skip the Surveillance By Opting Out of Face Recognition At Airports - EFF

items.name: Consider a secondary phone or laptop with minimal data
items.path: A separate, mostly empty device for the trip
items.why: If you have specific reason to think a border agent might attempt to forensically extract data from your device, consider traveling with secondary devices and leave your phone & laptop at home.

steps.text: Use an older device or a cheap secondary one that supports the apps you need
Set it up without your usual Apple or Google account to avoid syncing your data to it
Install only what you need for travel and avoid signing into your main accounts
If a secondary device isn't a realistic option, an alternative is to back up your regular device to a computer, factory reset your device, then restore from backup once you're back home

items.name: Use a VPN for airport wifi
items.why: It's generally advisable to avoid using airport wifi while you're traveling, but that's often unavoidable. If you must use the airport wifi, first connect to a VPN service and browse the internet only while connected to the VPN.

steps.text: Some popular VPN options are Proton, Mullvad, and IVPN
